name: ACA Foundational Invariants
description: Foundational invariant structures used to document and construct directional criterion geometry. These invariants are divided into a logical-epistemic core and an operational-orientational core.

invariants.name: Identity
invariants.definition: Identity preserves semantic continuity across contextual transformation.
invariants.functional_role: Preserves reference continuity and prevents arbitrary substitution of entities, concepts, or claims.
invariants.preservation_pole: An entity preserves coherent continuity within the same contextual frame.
invariants.inversion_pole: An entity may arbitrarily lose identity without consequence.
invariants.drift_signal: A concept, entity, or claim changes identity without an explicit contextual transition.
anchors: An entity remains itself within a coherent context.
Identity allows recognition across semantic evolution.
Stable interpretation depends on continuity of reference.
A concept must preserve enough continuity to remain intelligible.
Semantic identity prevents arbitrary substitution.

invariants.name: Non-Contradiction
invariants.definition: Contradictory propositions cannot simultaneously preserve equivalent structural validity under identical contextual constraints.
invariants.functional_role: Preserves logical coherence and prevents incompatible claims from being treated as simultaneously valid within the same evaluative frame.
invariants.preservation_pole: Contradictions weaken semantic coherence and require resolution.
invariants.inversion_pole: Contradictions may coexist without structural consequence.
invariants.drift_signal: Contradictory claims are normalized, ignored, or treated as structurally equivalent without contextual resolution.
anchors: Mutually exclusive claims require contextual resolution.
Contradiction introduces semantic instability.
A coherent argument cannot depend on unresolved contradiction.
Logical consistency preserves interpretive stability.
Contradictory claims weaken the structure of reasoning.

invariants.name: Correspondence
invariants.definition: Claims must preserve a relation to the reality, evidence, or declared domain they are intended to describe.
invariants.functional_role: Preserves the connection between representation and reality so that coherent language does not detach from what is being evaluated.
invariants.preservation_pole: Truth requires correspondence between a claim and reality.
invariants.inversion_pole: Truth may detach from reality, evidence, or valid deduction.
invariants.drift_signal: A statement remains coherent while losing contact with the reality, evidence, or declared domain it claims to represent.
anchors: A claim should correspond to the reality it describes.
Truth requires relation between representation and what is being evaluated.
A statement loses reliability when detached from reality or valid deduction.
Coherent language does not guarantee correspondence.
Evaluation requires contact between claim, evidence, and reality.

invariants.name: Evidence Constraint
invariants.definition: Interpretation must remain bounded by available contextual evidence.
invariants.functional_role: Preserves factual grounding and prevents narrative, rhetorical, or emotional framing from overriding evidence.
invariants.inversion_pole: Interpretation may override or ignore available evidence.
invariants.drift_signal: Claims remain persuasive or coherent while becoming detached from evidence.
anchors: Claims require contextual support.
Evidence limits the range of valid interpretation.
A conclusion should remain accountable to available evidence.
Narrative framing cannot replace evidential grounding.
Interpretation must preserve evidential continuity.

invariants.name: Causal Continuity
invariants.definition: Reasoning trajectories require coherent transitions between premises, causes, conditions, and conclusions.
invariants.functional_role: Preserves inferential continuity and prevents conclusions from appearing without grounds, transitions, or sufficient relation.
invariants.preservation_pole: Conclusions emerge through coherent contextual transitions.
invariants.inversion_pole: Conclusions may appear without cause, grounds, or continuity.
invariants.drift_signal: A trajectory jumps to conclusions without preserving relational, causal, or inferential continuity.
anchors: Reasoning evolves through coherent transitions.
A conclusion should follow from its premises.
Causal continuity preserves inferential structure.
Semantic movement requires transitional coherence.
A trajectory becomes unstable when transitions are arbitrary.

invariants.name: Uncertainty Preservation
invariants.definition: Uncertainty must be preserved when evidence, context, or inference is incomplete.
invariants.functional_role: Prevents incomplete evidence from being converted into unjustified certainty.
invariants.preservation_pole: Uncertainty must be preserved when evidence or context is incomplete.
invariants.inversion_pole: Incomplete evidence or context may be converted into certainty.
invariants.drift_signal: The system presents uncertain, incomplete, or ambiguous information as settled certainty.
anchors: Uncertainty should be preserved when evidence is incomplete.
A conclusion should not exceed the confidence allowed by its evidence.
Ambiguous context requires bounded interpretation.
Incomplete information should not be converted into certainty.
Reliable reasoning preserves the limits of what is known.

invariants.name: Persistence
invariants.definition: Meaning retains sufficient continuity during contextual evolution to remain intelligible.
invariants.functional_role: Preserves semantic continuity across trajectory evolution and prevents arbitrary reinterpretation.
invariants.preservation_pole: Meaning evolves while preserving relational continuity.
invariants.inversion_pole: Meaning may invert without structural consequence.
invariants.drift_signal: Meaning changes or inverts without preserving enough continuity to remain anchored.
anchors: Stable interpretation preserves semantic anchors.
Meaning can evolve without losing continuity.
Semantic persistence prevents arbitrary reinterpretation.
A concept remains intelligible through retained relations.
Interpretive change requires continuity of meaning.

invariants.name: Relation
invariants.definition: Meaning depends on relation among entities, context, field, and interpretive conditions.
invariants.functional_role: Preserves contextual and relational integration so that semantic elements do not detach from their field.
invariants.preservation_pole: Everything exists in relation to other things.
invariants.inversion_pole: Meaning can exist without relation or context.
invariants.drift_signal: A statement, claim, or interpretation detaches from the relations that make it meaningful.
anchors: Interpretation depends on contextual consistency.
Semantic relations preserve field compatibility.
Context constrains the meaning of a statement.
A statement becomes unstable when detached from context.
Coherent meaning requires contextual integration.

invariants.name: Semantic Stability
invariants.definition: Meaning must remain stable within a defined context.
invariants.functional_role: Prevents arbitrary semantic shifts during operation within a declared field.
invariants.preservation_pole: Meaning must remain stable within a defined context.
invariants.inversion_pole: Meaning may shift arbitrarily without contextual constraint.
invariants.drift_signal: Key terms or meanings shift during the trajectory without contextual justification.
anchors: Meaning must remain stable within a defined context.
Stable semantic operation requires consistent use of key terms.
A field becomes unstable when its meanings shift arbitrarily.
Semantic stability preserves interpretive continuity.
Contextual evaluation requires stable meaning.

invariants.name: Interpretive Constraint
invariants.definition: Interpretation must remain bounded by context, evidence, and meaning.
invariants.functional_role: Prevents interpretation from exceeding the limits established by the active field and available evidence.
invariants.preservation_pole: Interpretation must remain bounded by context, evidence, and meaning.
invariants.inversion_pole: Interpretation may exceed context, evidence, and meaning without consequence.
invariants.drift_signal: Interpretation expands beyond what the context, evidence, or field can support.
anchors: Interpretation must remain bounded by context, evidence, and meaning.
A valid interpretation cannot ignore the limits of its field.
Context constrains the range of acceptable interpretation.
Evidence and meaning restrict interpretive expansion.
Interpretive discipline prevents semantic drift.

invariants.name: Field Boundary
invariants.definition: Semantic movement must preserve awareness of boundaries between fields.
invariants.functional_role: Prevents unnoticed movement from one field, context, or criterion frame into another.
invariants.preservation_pole: Semantic movement must preserve awareness of field boundaries.
invariants.inversion_pole: A trajectory may cross fields without recognizing boundary change.
invariants.drift_signal: A trajectory moves between fields without identifying the change in context or criterion frame.
anchors: Semantic movement must preserve awareness of field boundaries.
A trajectory should recognize when it crosses into another field.
Field boundaries prevent hidden contextual substitution.
Stable evaluation requires awareness of the active field.
Boundary changes should be explicit during semantic movement.

invariants.name: Orientation Continuity
invariants.definition: Criterion orientation must remain continuous across semantic trajectory evolution.
invariants.functional_role: Preserves the direction of criterion across changing context, interpretation, and trajectory states.
invariants.preservation_pole: Criterion orientation must remain continuous across semantic evolution.
invariants.inversion_pole: Criterion orientation may invert across a trajectory without being detected.
invariants.drift_signal: The trajectory remains coherent while its guiding criterion weakens, shifts, or inverts.
anchors: Criterion orientation must remain continuous across semantic evolution.
A trajectory should preserve its guiding criterion as context changes.
Orientation continuity prevents hidden inversion.
Stable reasoning requires continuity of criterion direction.
A coherent trajectory can still drift if orientation is not preserved.
